As DNA storage gains momentum, managing its underlying data structure becomes a pressing concern. One area that demands improvement is the hierarchy and information arrangement, which significantly affects storage efficiency and retrieval speed. Currently, assigning locations to '0's and '1's in DNA storage is done randomly, resulting in suboptimal storage capacity and prolonged search times. This paper introduces a novel, location-assisted and island-based strategy that optimizes storage hierarchy and information arrangement, leading to a 400-fold reduction in search time and storage capacity improvement by up to 6 bits. Additionally, this method exhibits superior performance when combining data types, showcasing a 13 times improvement in search time when compared to existing approaches. The proposed technique's limitations are addressed by developing a dynamic, location-assisted and island-based algorithm that adapts to changing storage conditions, resulting in comparable performance to a theoretically ideal scenario. The proposed solutions were validated through comprehensive simulations and verified to be practical with real-world nanotechnology. The findings and techniques presented in this research can be applied to various storage hierarchies and data structures, and the associated source code is available online. The average storage capacity achieved was 6 bits per nucleotide, with maximum and minimum capacities recorded as 11 and 2 bits per nucleotide respectively. The average search time was 0.25 seconds, with maximum and minimum search times recorded as 1 and 0.1 seconds respectively. The proposed solutions were found to be compatible with multiple sequencing technologies, and the average storage efficiency was 75%, with maximum and minimum efficiencies recorded as 90 and 60% respectively. The average sequence error rate was 10 to the power of negative 6, with maximum and minimum error rates recorded as 10 to the power of negative 5 and 10 to the power of negative 7 respectively. The proposed solutions were further validated by applying them to real-world datasets, resulting in improved storage and search performance. The findings presented in this research have significant implications for the development of efficient and scalable DNA storage systems. High-dynamic-range photography is a well-established technique in photography that offers a more accurate visual representation by capturing a wider range of lighting levels than a single image can convey.  Despite its numerous benefits, HDR imaging has not seen widespread use due to the need for specialized equipment and complex post-processing techniques.  In recent years, smartphone cameras have become increasingly capable of capturing high-quality HDR images through a feature called HDR mode.  However, users have limited control over HDR mode, and the automatic HDR mode available on smartphones has a tendency to overexpose resulting images.  Overexposure is a significant issue in HDR photography as it can limit the range of tonal values captured within the image.  In this paper, a novel algorithm is presented that addresses overexposure in HDR photography by utilizing two images captured at different exposure levels.  The proposed technique employs image fusion to produce a single HDR image with a wider dynamic range than either individual image.  Overexposure is mitigated through a statistical analysis of the image's histogram, and a decision-making framework is developed to determine optimal exposure levels for HDR capture.  Experimental results indicate that the proposed technique yields HDR images with a wider dynamic range and reduced overexposure compared to standard HDR capture techniques.  Further testing revealed that the proposed technique can effectively handle challenging lighting conditions, producing HDR images with a wider dynamic range than conventional techniques and comparable to commercial smartphone HDR capture modes.  The proposed algorithm's efficiency was also validated through a computational analysis, and potential areas for optimization were identified.  The proposed technique's limitations and potential avenues for improvement were discussed, along with suggestions for further research and development.  The algorithm's source code has been made publicly available on GitHub, and experimental data has been uploaded to a public repository for review.  In conclusion, the proposed technique offers a reliable and efficient solution for capturing HDR images on smartphones, providing users with greater control over the exposure levels used in HDR capture and image fusion.  Further development of the algorithm is necessary to address issues with noise and chromatic aberration in captured HDR images.  The proposed technique has been put into practice through a mobile application developed for Android devices, and feedback from users has been collected and analyzed. Deep learning models have proven highly effective in accurately classifying and predicting data, yet the underlying mechanisms behind their ability to generalize remain poorly understood. The concept of overfitting, where a model excels at describing training data but fails to make accurate predictions on new data, presents a significant challenge for traditional machine learning methods but is navigated with ease by deep learning models due to their inherent capacity for generalization. The prevailing perspective views the relationship between training data and model capacity as linear, with the idea that deep learning models' vast capacity causes them to overfit unless regularization techniques are employed. This perspective overlooks the intrinsic connection between optimization algorithms used to train these models and the discovery of meaningful features in data, which is critical for generalization. The paper navigates this issue from a causal learning perspective, shedding light on the connection between optimization algorithms, models, and data, and explicitly defining conditions under which deep learning models exhibit optimal generalization performance. By doing so, it provides a theoretical foundation for the widespread success of deep learning models without relying on regularization techniques. The paper also introduces a metric called effective model complexity, which can be used to assess generalization performance in new data settings. The findings can be applied across various domains, including supervised and unsupervised learning, neural network training, and autotasking multiple deep learning models. The paper concludes by exploring the implications of its findings for the design of optimization algorithms, neural networks, and multiple learning models, offering a roadmap for future research. This study examines a nonlinear, history-dependent cardiac mechanics model that is subject to large deformations and electromechanical interactions. To ensure the numerical stability and convergence of the finite element method, we investigated various scalable multilevel preconditioning techniques for their effectiveness in solving the nonlinear system of equations resulting from the cardiac mechanics model. Specifically, we assessed the performance of three distinct approaches: a traditional direct method, a block-diagonal preconditioner constructed using a multilevel process, and a Schur complement reduction technique employed at different levels of complexity. Our numerical experiments, conducted using realistic heart tissue models and imaging data, were performed on multiple processor cores and yielded comparable results in terms of computational efficiency. Notably, the models adhered strictly to the principles of material frame indifference, and we validated the numerical solutions by verifying that the governing balance equations and the conservation of momentum hold exactly in the discrete sense. Continuous optimization is a crucial aspect in various settings such as contextual marketing, supply chains, and energy management. These processes have multiple objectives that are difficult to balance and change over time, necessitating the use of sequential decision-making techniques. A critical step in developing practical applications involves evaluating the performance of these processes over time. In contrast to evaluating processes over a fixed time period, evaluating processes that continue indefinitely is a more challenging task. In such processes, past decisions can influence current and future outcomes, making it difficult to accurately assess the impact of different evaluation methods. Existing research primarily focuses on evaluating processes over a fixed time period, and only a few consider processes that continue indefinitely. In response to this challenge, we present a dynamic evaluation framework called L2Explorer that assesses the performance of processes that continue indefinitely. This framework enables us to compare and distinguish between different evaluation methods based on the underlying dynamics of the processes. We demonstrate the practical application of L2Explorer in a contextual marketing setting and show that it can effectively compare the performance of different evaluation methods, some of which are widely used in practice but lack a theoretical basis. We also explore the theoretical boundaries of which evaluation methods are superior in certain dynamic conditions. By developing L2Explorer, we provide a foundation for evaluating processes that continue indefinitely and identify opportunities for improving existing evaluation methods. These improvements could lead to better contextual marketing policies that balance short-term and long-term rewards. We make L2Explorer available online at https://l2explorer.com/.

We propose a method to extract features from lung images that correlate with a patient's criticality, as measured by their SAPS II score.  To validate our approach, we employed a synthetic dataset that mimicked real-world imaging and clinical data.  However, some researchers have expressed concerns that such an approach may inadvertently introduce bias in the machine learning model.  To address this concern, we created a second, purely synthetic dataset that excluded any reference to patient outcomes in the imaging data.  Both datasets yielded comparable results, indicating that image features alone are sufficient for accurately predicting patient outcomes.  To further illustrate the significance of image features beyond what is captured in SAPS II, we employed a method to identify which image features are unique to each dataset.  Interestingly, certain features consistently emerged as significant across both datasets, suggesting that they hold critical importance in determining patient outcomes.  To apply this insight in a practical setting, we conducted an experiment in which we used a support vector machine to distinguish between two groups of patients with differing outcomes, using only the unique image features.  The results showed that image features alone can differentiate between high and low-risk patients with a 90% accuracy rate. The concept of a simplicial bundle can be defined using simplicial maps that satisfy local triviality properties. We demonstrate that a simplicial space over another space can be equipped with a simplicial bundle structure, specifically topological, without relying on classical bundle theory. This result extends a previous finding by Grandis and Lucà for simplicial spaces defined by simplicial maps that form a simplicial multivaluation. Moreover, it is shown that using classical bundle theory is equivalent to using simplicial methods to define a simplicial space with local sections. A characterization of simplicial spaces with local sections is also established, along with a connection to the concept of simplicial valuations. Lastly, we explore how simplicial spaces defined by simplicial maps that form a simplicial multivaluation can be obtained from simplicial spaces defined by simplicial maps that form a multivaluation through quotient construction.

In recent years, advances have been made in visual association detection tasks due to the use of convolutional neural networks. These networks enable the mapping of input images to output words without the restriction of sequential ordering. Current approaches typically employ recurrent neural networks to model associations, which can result in incorrect positive classifications by misinterpreting the network's capacity to map images to words independently. This study proposes an alternative method that uses a network to directly predict the association probability from the interaction between the input image and word, which is represented as a learned vector. By designing the network to distinguish between independent and interdependent associations, it accurately identifies the erroneous positive classifications commonly seen in current methods. Experimental results show that this proposed approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on the CaffeFP and MinKIT-100 datasets and achieves comparable performance on the VGGFP dataset. Additionally, it is observed that this method can be effectively trained using a contrastive hard negative mining loss, which enhances the network's ability to capture the intrinsic difficulties of certain dataset instances. This is demonstrated by its ability to distinguish between easily and difficultly learned positive classifications on the MinKIT-100 dataset. This is a fundamental approach that can be integrated into existing methods by training the network to recognize the specific distribution of a particular dataset, which enhances the performance of current methods on various benchmark datasets used for object detection and instance-level scene parsing. This approach is also a starting point for exploring the use of word embeddings in visual association detection tasks. This approach has been made available on GitHub for public use. Deepfake technology and counterfeit news are rapidly evolving and are difficult to detect manually. These counterfeits are not limited to being created but are also continually evolving, necessitating a dynamic approach to their detection. In response to this challenge, we introduce a novel task called context-adaptive counterfeiting detection, where the context refers to the continuously emerging deepfake or counterfeit news. We propose a new framework called MetaMMC-Net to address this task. This framework combines the capabilities of meta-learning to tackle context-adaptability and multimodal neural networks to handle image-text-based counterfeiting detection. We employ a neural process approach to incorporate a query context into the model, enabling it to learn a context-conditional distribution that adapts to unfamiliar contexts. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method on the current counterfeiting data before evaluating its performance on emerging counterfeits. Our results show that MetaMMC-Net achieves superior performance compared to baseline models on the recently introduced Multi-EmeNet dataset and outperforms existing single-model counterfeiting detection benchmarks. We also analyze the influence of image-text imbalances and extraction techniques on the model's performance and propose feasible solutions to these problems. Our proposed method and experimental results pave the way for further investigation into the context-adaptive deepfake detection task. We publicly release our code and data balancing techniques at https://github.com/zhengyangzeng/MetaMMC-Net.

The homotopy theory of a certain class of spaces, known as infinite highly connected CW-complexes, serves as the foundation for a specific mathematical construction called stable homotopy theory. By employing Bousfield-Kan's simplicial symmetric monoidal category, we develop a systematic method for counting and analyzing infinite grouped partitions of infinite highly connected CW-complexes. As a key application, we derive an explicit formula for computing the number of distinct ordered partitions across multiple infinite highly connected CW-complexes. Furthermore, we establish connections between these counting problems and established results in enumerative combinatorial analysis. Alongside, we outline a procedure for generating polynomial equations whose solutions correspond to the ordered partitions of a specified infinite highly connected CW-complex. As a specific example, we calculate the partition polynomial for an infinitely complex space constructed from a single point. Alongside, we explore connections to established formulas in classical combinatorial analysis and provide an enumerative interpretation of a notable polynomial equation known as the Frobeneius-Dedekind reciprocity law. As a supplementary result, we establish a method for generating counting polynomials for a broader class of spaces known as infinite weakly connected CW-complexes. As a key result, we derive a formula for counting the distinct ordered partitions of an infinite weakly connected CW-complex and demonstrate that this formula aligns with an established result in combinatorial analysis known as the MacMahon master theorem. Alongside, we discuss the enumerative significance of this combinatorial formula and provide an alternative proof based on enumerative combinatorial analysis. As a broader context, we outline the relationship between the counting polynomials of infinite highly connected CW-complexes and a class of polynomial equations known as hypersurface Frobeneius equations. As a key result, we establish that the counting polynomials of infinite highly connected CW-complexes can be viewed as solutions to a specific subcategory of the hypersurface Frobeneius equations known as the absolute Frobeneius equations. As a supplementary context, we outline the relationship between the counting polynomials of infinite weakly connected CW-complexes and a class of polynomial equations known as extended hypersurface Frobeneius equations. As a key result, we derive a method for generating the counting polynomials of infinite weakly connected CW-complexes from the solutions of the absolute Frobeneius equations and demonstrate that these counting polynomials align with the results of the enumerative combinatorial analysis known as the MacMahon master theorem.

A significant challenge in treating stroke lies in creating effective treatment plans. This paper aims to enhance MRI-based cerebral lesion prediction by leveraging a sophisticated neural network called PVAE. Developed specifically for medical applications, PVAE combines the benefits of Variational Auto-Encoders and Generative Adversarial Networks to accurately identify and forecast cerebral lesions on MRI scans. Through rigorous testing on public datasets, our model demonstrates superior performance compared to established techniques, achieving a 94.67% classification accuracy in predicting lesion presence and a Mean Squared Error of 0.032 in forecasting lesion extent. Furthermore, an in-depth analysis of model performance reveals that both its encoder and decoder components are equally vital for optimal results. To take it a step further, the PVAE framework has been modified to accommodate multi-modal data, seamlessly integrating different MRI scan types while maintaining excellent performance. To create a realistic simulation environment for future research, a comprehensive dataset has been developed comprising 2000 cerebral lesion scans with varying sizes and shapes. This model has been put forward as a starting point for developing novel treatment plans rather than a definitive solution, with areas for improvement identified and potential enhancements to the model discussed. GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient data processing, especially for tasks involving graph-structured data. It serves as a general-purpose programming paradigm that outperforms traditional imperative languages in certain computational domains, such as social network analysis and graph algorithms. However, implementing GP 2 programs on GP 2 requires significant effort due to the complexity of its type system and lack of available tools. To address this challenge, we developed the GP 2 compiler, a comprehensive and user-friendly platform that includes a type checker, compiler, and runtime environment. The compiler's advanced features, combined with its efficient runtime environment, enable fast execution of GP 2 programs on top of GP 2. To demonstrate the compiler's versatility and benefits, we created a set of test programs and measured their execution speeds both with and without the compiler. Our results show that compiling GP 2 programs yields a significant performance improvement, in some cases exceeding 100-fold. To further illustrate the compiler's utility, we utilized the Eclipse GP 2 environment to develop and test a real-world application, a shortest path algorithm for complex graphs. The resulting GP 2 program exhibits excellent performance, outperforming its equivalent Java implementation by approximately 20x. The Eclipse GP 2 environment, available at https://github.com/EnhancedGP2/EclipseGP2, includes the compiler, runtime environment, and development tools for creating and testing GP 2 programs. To facilitate easier transition from GP 2 programs to the compiler, we developed a simple pre-compiler that converts standard GP 2 syntax into the compiler's expected format. The pre-compiler, available at https://github.com/EnhancedGP2/GP2-Precompiler, enables seamless integration with the compiler, allowing for efficient execution of GP 2 programs on top of GP 2 without the need for manual conversion. The Enhanced GP 2 Compiler received the Outstanding Student Paper Award at the 2023 International Conference on Computational Science.

In recent years, attribute extraction has seen significant progress, with many approaches being trial and error due to the lack of labeled attribute data. A common issue with existing methods is the need to predetermine the attribute categories' structure, which can be complicated by the limited information available. In contrast, a linear structure can be determined after learning the attributes, as demonstrated by recent research using multi-task learning and score-based methods. However, both of these current paradigms rely heavily on the quality of their initial query samples, which can compromise performance when the number of attributes is large and the number of samples is limited. A new framework called U-SAGE is proposed, leveraging a unified linear structure that combines the dual form of attribute and a contrastive learning-based rejection mechanism to enhance the model's ability to distinguish between attributes and reject background noise, resulting in U-SAGE outperforming current state-of-the-art methods on three benchmark datasets. When applied to a linear structure, U-SAGE achieves a 6.3% relative improvement in the mean of the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve when the number of attributes is large and the number of samples is limited, demonstrating its versatility and ability to adapt to unknown data structures. U-SAGE's simplicity and versatility also make it an attractive choice for extending attribute extraction to new, previously unseen categories, as shown by a 10.3% relative improvement in the mean of the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve when the number of samples is limited. It has been observed that for any given positive integer d, there is a subsequence of WN_n(k) convergence whose local properties at vertices of degree d are equivalent to those found in a specific random network. Notably, this includes a subsequence whose limit network at those degrees resembles a twisted wreath structure for any d greater than two. Additionally, we discover that the infinite sequence WN_n(k) is distinguishable from another known network structure, specifically those with a 2-twisted star quotient network. Working with categorical data for regression tasks is common, and it often involves dealing with variables that have a large number of levels. In such cases, selecting relevant categories can greatly improve model performance. We propose a new Group Lasso-based method, called CategLasso, to identify and eliminate unnecessary categories by introducing a specific strategy to handle dummy variables created from categorical data. Unlike existing approaches that treat each level of a category as a continuous variable, our method uses a sparse group lasso framework to find the minimal number of levels required for each category. We demonstrate through extensive simulations that CategLasso achieves comparable or better performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, especially when the number of levels per category is small. We also apply CategLasso to real-world datasets, and the results show that it can effectively reduce dimensions and improve accuracy in various datasets, including genetic data and customer segmentation data. We offer a Python implementation of CategLasso on GitHub, along with example usage and real-world application code. By leveraging a data-driven approach to determine the number of levels per category, we are able to identify instances where CategLasso reduces the number of levels by eliminating unnecessary intermediate levels while retaining all extreme and pivotal levels, which is crucial in capturing essential information from the data. This is particularly important in datasets with genetic or categorical variables, which often have a hierarchical structure. This hierarchical structure can result in up to $O(p^2)$ features when there are $p$ variables, which can lead to $p^2$ coefficients in the regression model, making it difficult to apply conventional machine learning methods. We provide a computational example to illustrate this challenge. We also explore ways to further sparsify CategLasso by introducing a data-driven approach to define a compact set of levels for each category, which enables us to extend the method to handle large datasets with a hierarchical structure. This is achieved by incorporating a new hyperparameter that allows for the selection of the minimum number of levels required for each category, which results in a generalized version of the method called gCategLasso. We apply gCategLasso to real-world datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in capturing the hierarchical structure of the data. We also provide a theoretical guarantee for the stability of gCategLasso by proving that it satisfies a restricted strong convexity condition, which enables us to leverage existing convex optimization results to derive bounds on the estimation error. High-resolution vector maps are gaining popularity in various applications such as driving and navigation, but they often result in performance issues due to computational demands and limited processing power. In this paper, an efficient anti-aliasing technique for rendering lines on vector maps is presented. By utilizing a spatial alpha map and a simplified coverage testing method, a significant reduction in rendering time and memory consumption is achieved. The proposed algorithm's efficiency has been tested and compared to existing anti-aliasing techniques through real-time rendering of a large-scale map on various platforms, demonstrating its superior performance. The proposed technique has been implemented in a popular web rendering engine, resulting in a 3x to 5x reduction in rendering time for line connections and enabling the use of high-quality anti-aliasing in various applications. The proposed algorithm can also be applied to the rendering of lines in games and other graphics-related fields. The code for the proposed technique has been made available online.

In multi-channel speech processing, separating and enhancing the individual channels can significantly improve the signal-to-noise ratio and overall speech intelligibility. This task becomes particularly challenging when only a single mixure signal is available for input, as seen in single-microphone scenarios. To address this issue, we propose the Dual-Path Convolutional Recurrent Network (DPCRN) architecture, which takes advantage of both time and frequency domain information to separately enhance each individual channel. The DPCRN model consists of two parallel paths: a recurrent neural network (RNN) that handles sequence dependencies and convolutional neural networks (CNN) that capture local patterns in both the time and frequency domains. We experiment with the DPCRN architecture on the INTERSPEECH 2019 ASA task and observe a 2.0 dB improvement in the signal-to-distortion ratio (SDR) compared to the baseline Conv-TASNet model. Additionally, we evaluate the proposed DPCRN architecture on the INTERSPEECH 2020 DNS challenge and achieve a 5.1 dB enhancement in the SDR, outperforming the current state-of-the-art models.

By using the Bozhilov complex plane metric, we find that the real part of the phase angle $\phi_r$ affects the shadow's shape significantly, while the imaginary part $\phi_i$ has a minimal impact. Moreover, we examine how both the nonlinearity and the phase angle influence the shadow's area and temperature. These analyses can be verified numerically and analytically. The study presents a tomographic representation made up of 16 moments for a 3-dimensional Banach space, which accurately describes any quantum state. We leverage this representation to investigate the correlation between entanglement and synchronization in a scenario featuring two parametrically changed bosonic systems in a 3-dimensional Banach space. We determine the conditions under which the tomographic map maintains its nonentanglement properties and provide an algorithm for calculating the minimum number of entanglement parameters required to capture the complex dynamics of the two systems. We further develop an indicator that monitors the onset of synchronization by tracking changes in the tomographic map's average value. Our findings are applicable to both continuous-variable soliton states and any two parametrically changed systems in a 3-dimensional Banach space. We believe that our approach offers a practical solution for detecting the onset of synchronization and measuring the degree of entanglement in continuous-variable systems based on the tomogram of one system only. We also provide a theoretical framework that can be tested and confirmed by performing a tomographic analysis of the two systems in their joint state. Creating engaging, dynamic, and interactive 360-degree virtual travel videos requires precise control over the viewer's perspective.  To achieve this, a forecasting framework for the target viewport is necessary.  Existing methods primarily focus on predicting the future viewport based on past data, neglecting the significance of provided subtitles that offer valuable context.  In this paper, we introduce a novel viewport forecasting approach that incorporates the meaning of accompanying subtitles to enhance the predicted viewport.  Utilizing a multi-task convolutional neural network, the proposed method successfully takes into account the subtitles and delivers a more accurate viewport prediction.  To evaluate the method, we developed a 360-degree viewport forecasting dataset that incorporates subtitles, and our experiments show that incorporating subtitles in the model yields a notable improvement in forecasting performance.  The proposed approach has been applied in real-world scenarios to guide the viewer's perspective through dynamic and controlled movements, resulting in a more immersive viewing experience.  The code for the proposed approach has been made publicly available on GitHub.  To further facilitate research, we have made the 360-degree viewport forecasting dataset, consisting of subtitles and corresponding viewports, available for download.  In the accompanying video, we have visually presented the proposed approach's capability to incorporate subtitles and guide the viewer's perspective through dynamic and controlled movements, leading to a more engaging and immersive viewing experience.  The video has been uploaded to the arXiv website. Deep neural networks excel at various tasks with high accuracy, but there's a significant gap when it comes to out-of-domain performances. This issue can be mitigated by selecting a task-expert network that has high precision for a different task, but it's not always feasible due to limited access to multiple task-specific networks. This paper explores the concept of employing a single, universally trained decision network that has been taught to make high-confidence decisions with a 90% threshold. It's demonstrated that this decision network can be effectively utilized as a proxy to determine if a query sample belongs to a particular domain with precision levels comparable to a support network trained using a conventional paradigm. Furthermore, it's shown that this decision network can be leveraged to achieve comparable performance to traditional training methods in scenarios involving few-shot learning and domain adaptation. A universally trained decision network can be readily applicable across various applications, including, but not limited to, anomaly detection, where it can be employed to identify domain-specific samples with a 99.1% precision level. The proposed approach is scalable, efficient, and cost-effective as it eliminates the need for multiple task-specific networks, instead utilizing a single universally trained decision network that can be easily integrated into existing machine learning pipelines with minimal modifications. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of this approach in various scenarios, thereby providing a universally beneficial decision network that can be collectively utilized as a valuable asset across different machine learning domains. Code is available at: https://github.com/ghru/ZeroShotDecisionNetwork.

Using reinforcement learning to train neural machine translation models has shown promise, but its efficacy is significantly impaired by the vast action space posed by the vocabulary. We propose a novel method called Wordwise Reinforcement Learning (WRL), which divides the action space into smaller tasks of a much more manageable size, selecting the most suitable word for each position within the sequence. We employ a memory-efficient approach to store and update the policy's parameters, enabling WRL to be applied to both encoder-decoder models and left-to-right ones without significant computational or memory-related costs. Our proposed method cuts the reward's diminishing returns issue by introducing a focus mechanism that allows the model to prioritize the words surrounding the sequence's central areas. We achieve the best results when the focus is focused on the beginning of the sequence, but an evenly weighted average achieves comparable performance while being more robust. WRL's effectiveness is demonstrated by its ability to surpass the baseline's performance, and when combined with the coverage penalty, it is capable of surpassing the state-of-the-art NMT models. Moreover, we show that wordwise rewards can be leveraged for other tasks such as sentence planning and summarization generation. We call this approach Wordwise Reward Exploration (WRE) and demonstrate its capability to produce coherent summaries of up to 512 tokens in a single sequence. We recommend WRL and WRE for a variety of sequence generation tasks that involve the search for optimal orders within action spaces. We make the code available at https://github.com/ghru/wordwise-reinforcement-learning.

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, NoSQL database that has gained popularity in various production environments. Due to its lack of support for transactions across different databases, incorporating MongoDB into existing distributed database systems poses a challenge. In response to this limitation, we investigated MongoDB's transactional behavior within a single instance. Although existing research validates MongoDB's isolation levels, it falls short of examining the effect of various concurrent operations on MongoDB's data consistency. In this paper, we build upon the existing validation by creating a test suite that simulates a range of concurrent scenarios to ensure MongoDB's adherence to specific integrity properties. Our testing framework, available publicly, comprises over 200 test cases that validate MongoDB's compliance with key properties, including atomicity, consistency, durability, and isolation. By utilizing this test suite, we identified two integrity violations and proposed potential solutions to address these issues. Furthermore, we evaluated the performance impact of our suggested solutions and found them to incur minimal overhead on MongoDB's performance. In addition to our findings, we recognized that MongoDB exhibits unexpected behavior during rollback operations and uncovered the underlying cause, which we believe stems from its use of WiredTiger's snapshot isolation. In response to these discoveries, we propose a straightforward solution to rectify this issue by modifying MongoDB's transaction management layer. In conclusion, this paper provides a comprehensive validation of MongoDB's transactional behavior and offers actionable advice to guide its integration into existing distributed database systems. In particular, we recommend utilizing multi-document transactions with the readConcern: "majority" parameter to ensure data consistency in production environments that utilize MongoDB. This achievement is accompanied by an additional derivation of the double sum representation of the chromatic symmetric polynomials, as well as an examination of the particular case where the integers are consecutive. Furthermore, an expansion of the last mentioned kind contains the coefficients of the inverse Kostka matrix, offering a distinct proof of the established fact that these coefficients are nonnegative. Understanding the beam properties in the Drell-Yan production is crucial for accurately measuring the Higgs boson mass in the Thompson p$\bar{p}$ decay channel using the CDF II detector. To analyze the beam characteristics, a method has been developed to accurately determine the transverse size of the proton beam by measuring the distribution of scattered protons from the interaction between a circulating proton beam and a stationary proton target. To achieve this, a specialized scan of the transverse plane of the detector was performed, utilizing the CDF II detector's ability to precisely locate and measure the scattering points of protons within the dimensions of the beam. By analyzing the distribution of these scattering points, researchers have determined the transverse dimensions of the proton beam with a 0.1% level of accuracy, finding it to be approximately 3.73 millimeters in both the x and y directions. Additionally, the distribution of these scattering points has been utilized to identify the presence of a small-scale oscillation in the beam profile, resulting in a 0.3% level of additional error in the measurement of the Higgs boson mass. To mitigate this effect, a strategy has been proposed to reduce the beam scan dimensions and limit the impact of this oscillation on the measurement of the Higgs boson mass.

Understanding the instrumental effects that influence Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) data is crucial for extracting reliable information from current and future experiments. To facilitate this comprehension, we have developed the Python package's4cmb' to simulate the instrumental characteristics of CMB experiments and their impact on data, specifically for parallactic and multi-moded instruments. Here, we outline the capabilities of's4cmb' by describing its core components that simulate: the signal; the instrument's response; beam shapes; noise; and the effect of half-sample aliasing. As a comprehensive tool,'s4cmb' allows users to assess the influence of instrumental effects on observed signals and provides pre-built classes for specific experiments, along with customizable options for simulating any combination of instrumental characteristics. By offering detailed simulations of instrumental effects and aliasing,'s4cmb' can be a valuable resource for interpreting data from current and future CMB experiments, and for guiding the development of optimal analysis methods and signal processing techniques. The code is available online at its permanent repository address.

When given words that form a correct sentence, but in a different order than typically seen, BART struggles to return the more common order. In recent years, point cloud representations have gained significant popularity 
due to their versatility in 3D vision tasks. Researchers have successfully applied 
neural networks to these representations, achieving state-of-the-art results in 
various tasks such as classification, regression, and detection. Nonetheless, point 
cloud networks often suffer from sensitivity to limited training data, causing them
to exhibit poor generalization performance. To address this limitation, the field 
of point cloud learning has drawn inspiration from the concept of data augmentation
through transformations, which significantly improves the networks' ability to generalize.
However, applying these transformations results in a major issue: the points in 
the point cloud become correlated with the classification label, hindering effective 
training by modern optimization algorithms. To break this correlation, the paper 
introduces a novel smoothing technique called Transformation-Dependent Point Cloud 
Smoothing (TPC), which utilizes network-based transformations to train efficient, 
generalizable point cloud networks. Experimentation across various 3D vision tasks
demonstrates the efficacy of TPC, achieving superior results to the current state-of-
the-art methods. Moreover, the paper showcases the scalability and effectiveness 
of the TPC technique by successfully training a point cloud network on a massive 
classification dataset comprising over 1 million classes. The code for the paper 
is available at the following link: https://github.com/ghaith/TPC.

In recent years, Generative Adversarial Networks have been successfully applied in generating coherent and diverse texts. These models typically train a generator to produce text and a discriminator to differentiate between genuine and fabricated text. Since direct access to vast amounts of training data is often a limitation for certain text creation tasks, we've explored methods for training GAN-based text generators in controlled environments where one generator trains an opponent network to mimic their own generated text while the other generator attempts to distinguish between real and synthesized text. We've examined the performance of these setups in both sparse and semi-supervised learning configurations and found that, contrary to expectations, the generator that trains an opponent network to recognize their own text does not excel over conventional training methods. To address this issue, we've developed SparseGAN, a GAN-based text generator that trains an opponent network to act as a 'competent' adversary with the primary goal of becoming a proficient text generator. We've tested SparseGAN in both sparse and semi-supervised learning settings and observed notable improvements over conventional training methods. When generating text alone, SparseGAN exhibited a 13% relative improvement in BLEU score compared to the ATGAN baseline, while in a collaborative setting with another network, SparseGAN achieved a 21% relative improvement in our proposed diversity evaluation metric. The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another via panspermia has been a longstanding and captivating concept. To explore the validity of this hypothesis in the context of interstellar life, it's essential to determine if viable microbial life forms could withstand the extreme conditions of space and astrobiological influences during their interstellar journey. To assess this, we examined the viability of various microbial models using a viability function that considers the effects of low temperatures, ionizing radiation, and chemical exposure. By simulating the conditions encountered by microbes in different types of stars and their resulting habitable zones, we mapped the outcomes for a representative microbe in various astrophysical scenarios. Our findings suggest that the success of interstellar panspermia relies on the specific characteristics of the microbe, the environment of the star from which it originates, and the conditions it's exposed to during its journey. However, our simulations indicate that even in the most inhospitable star systems, there are regions where microbes could take root and thrive, implying that the transfer of life from one system to another might not be purely impossible after all. To further investigate this hypothesis, we propose a more in-depth examination of the relationships between microbial diversity, the conditions of the parent star, and the outcomes of interstellar panspermia. By exploring these connections, we can gain a better understanding of whether and how the transfer of life between systems could occur.

By developing a reduced model that accounts for the slow evolution of the phase difference between connected populations, we identify key conditions for transmission, block formation, and complete synchronization in multilayer networks, as well as explore various configurations and interlayer coupling strengths to observe the resulting synchronized patterns. Our study extends the previous single-layer analysis to a broader, multilayer framework, offering a comprehensive framework for understanding the complex dynamics of synchronized patterns in networks of coupled oscillators.

By incorporating a thin layer of Mn3NiN between two magnetic layers with opposite magnetic orientations, researchers have found that the Nernst effect can switch the magnetic moments in two different ways, either synchronizing with the temperature-dependent magnetic orientation or reversing it. This unique behavior allows for the creation of a magnetic memory element that can recall both its magnetic orientation and the temperature it was trained on, a capability that could be utilized in advanced temperature-sensing and memory storage devices. We establish the global existence, uniform boundedness, and asymptotic behavior of solutions to these systems, even in the presence of moving barriers. This achievement holds true for a wide range of dynamically shifting Hamiltonian functions that satisfy certain growth rate requirements. Our main contribution builds upon previous work by allowing more extensive types of dynamically changing Hamiltonian functions and expanding the range of possible growth rates compared to previous studies. Our solutions to these systems, even with moving barriers, also exhibit improved asymptotic behavior. We achieve these results by utilizing a newly developed approach that applies a modified version of the differential identity established by Nishikawa. Our findings are further illustrated with a numerical example. Our work offers a potential application to controlling the behavior of nonlinear systems subject to delays. Our research also offers a potential extension to studying similar systems defined on unbounded domains. Our article concludes by exploring the connection between these systems and related problems involving second-order time-dependent mean field games. A self-sensing harmonic contour identification method is developed for composites using electrical impedance tomography (EIT). As a key feature in condition monitoring, identifying harmonic contours is crucial, but it requires precise impedance data, which can be challenging to obtain in self-sensing materials. The proposed approach utilizes evolutionary algorithms to determine the exact location of harmonic contours in EIT images with the minimum possible error, eliminating the necessity for precise impedance data. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through both numerical and experimental investigations. Numerical simulations with added noise are used to evaluate the algorithm's performance, and it shows excellent results even with high levels of measurement errors. A carbon fiber reinforced polymer plate with a known harmonic contour serves as the test subject in the experimental study. The results from the algorithm yield a perfect match with the known contour when noise is minimal but less accurate when measurement noise is substantial. The proposed method's limitations and potential areas for improvement are also discussed. The developed framework's potential applications are broad and it could be adapted for use in other condition monitoring scenarios. The code for the algorithm is provided in the supplementary materials. The findings also contribute to the advancement of harmonic contour identification in inverse problems through evolutionary algorithms. The proposed method can be improved further, for instance, by using more advanced evolutionary algorithms or combining it with machine learning techniques, which could enhance its performance and accuracy. The developed framework has the potential to be adapted for use in other imaging and inverse problems, such as magnetic resonance imaging, optical imaging, and seismic imaging, among others. Understanding how the brain controls walking involves not only recognizing the neural signals associated with ambulatory states but also deciphering the underlying step frequency information. In this study, we used electrocorticogram signals recorded from the precentral cortex of a paraplegic patient whose spinal cord was injured at level Th6. We gathered over 500 minutes of data during two sessions in which the patient stood with the help of a harness. We extracted features from EEG data based on time-frequency methods and used these to estimate the step frequency and ambulatory states. Our results showed that we could accurately identify the patient's step frequency and determine when he was walking or standing still. Our research provides a clear example of how the brain generates walking and standing information and offers a tangible solution for developing brain-machine interfaces that control walking. In its current form, our model lasts for approximately 30 minutes without being recalibrated, but with further development, it has the potential to be a long-term solution for patients with similar spinal cord injuries. In future work, we plan to apply this method to patients with less severe injuries and explore ways to develop more advanced models that can provide longer-term data and better step frequency information. In its current state, our model assumes a fixed rest and walking state duration, but we also explored an alternative method that calculated these durations from the data and found that it resulted in similar outcomes. In the course of this research, we encountered an issue with overfitting that we addressed by implementing a data-driven approach to determine the optimal parameters for our models. In the next phase of this project, we aim to apply these methods to new areas of study such as the paraplegic patient's arm movements and the effects of sensory feedback on their walking. In the process of analyzing the data, we discovered that the patient's EEG signals during walking contained a specific frequency that remained present even after he stopped moving, but we also found that it took him a noticeable amount of time to start moving again after he was displaced. Belegradek recently demonstrated that every subgroup of a right-angled Artin group that is generated by subgenerators has a left invariant metric. In the present research, we establish that only divisions generated by left invariant metrics exist within right-angled Artin groups. This conclusion can be obtained by applying the results of Guirardel and Levasque to a specific graph whose properties are characterized. Furthermore, we show that two distinct subgroups generated by subgenerators of a right-angled Artin group can have different isomorphism types, thereby confirming a conjecture initially made by Tock. Additionally, we identify specific divisions that are not generated by left invariant metrics, thereby expanding upon Belegradek's initial classification. Lastly, we determine that the group of homeodimensional embeddings induced by a specific order on the finite subgroups of a right-angled Artin group is precisely the group of type B automorphisms, which in turn is equivalent to the statement that the division generated by finite subgroups is precisely the division defined by the order type B.

A new approach using connectivity estimation has been developed to automatically detect time-dependent connections within a system by constructing a distinct feature for each data point in time. This feature captures the probability of existing connections at a specific point in time and is calculated using a non-parametric estimator. The developed method was applied to a synthetic dataset with known properties and showed accurate results compared to a static analysis method. Furthermore, the approach was tested on real EEG data during a working memory task and yielded distinct temporal patterns of connectivity that aligned with task-related dynamics. The developed technique has been made available on GitHub for public use. Additionally, we investigate the method's suitability for specific applications, including linear least squares solutions and ridge regression. With the aim of exploiting Tensor Cores' capabilities fully, we also examine the generalization of the technique to accommodate half-precision bias terms in linear models. By incorporating a data preprocessing step, we demonstrate the method's effectiveness in these contexts. Evaluations are conducted using popular machine learning datasets, and the results are compared to conventional matrix inversion techniques. We have publicly available implementations of the proposed methods, along with sample datasets, for further exploration and optimization. The code is written in Python, utilizing CUDA and NVIDIA's Tensor Cores through the cuPy library. The research was supported by the National Science Foundation under grant IIS-1838047. The findings have significant implications for developing scalable linear regression models that leverage the speed and efficiency of NVIDIA Tensor Cores. The BLS08 signature scheme exhibits exceptional resistance to quantum attacks while maintaining satisfactory classical efficiency. However, its speed is hindered by the costly computation of point trim evaluations. We present an alternative, faster method for creating pseudorandom points that mimic the effect of point trim, thereby streamlining the BLS08 signature scheme implementation. Specifically, we substitute point trim with a shorter sequence of point multiplication operations by randomly selected curves, each comprising a different degree. This results in a signature of roughly 160 bytes, which can identify an anonymous message as belonging to a specific class, assuming that point trim behaves in a manner analogous to the proposed pseudorandomization method. Notably, this pseudorandomization method can be derived from knowledge of a secret key, thereby precluding forgery attempts. We further explore an application of this pseudorandomization method to enhance the efficiency of the Fujimura's scheme of quantum-aware message authentication, which yields a signature of roughly 192 bytes. We tested our implementation on the ARM Cortex-A53 processor and observed a 2-fold reduction in the signature generation time and a 4-fold increase in the verification time of the BLS08 scheme, compared to the original implementation. We also tested our implementation on the Intel Core i7-4770 processor and observed a 1.5-fold reduction in the signature generation time and a 2-fold increase in the verification time of the BLS08 scheme. We term the proposed pseudorandomization method as the "trim-isogeny" parameter, which can be derived from a secret key, and we make our implementation publicly available on GitHub. We discuss the possibility of creating the trim-isogeny parameter through an optimization of the degree-$n$ isogeny generation, which could further enhance the efficiency of the BLS08 signature scheme, although this would require the storage of $n$ separate curves, each of a different degree, which could exceed the available memory. We propose an alternative, more efficient approach to curve storage, which could alleviate this issue by storing a single curve and employing the trim-isogeny parameter to determine the corresponding curve and point, which would incur an additional memory cost of roughly 64 bytes. We term this approach as the "compressed trim-isogeny" parameter, which we found to enhance the efficiency of the BLS08 signature scheme, but we were unable to determine its precise impact, due to difficulties in implementing the compressed trim-isogeny parameter on existing hardware. The growing use of connected devices in various situations, with limited communication, necessitates the development of efficient linear bandit algorithms. In a recent study, a linear contextual bandit model with unknown parameters was explored, and an unbounded learning rate was established for an algorithm that relies solely on local observations and bounded estimates of the mean rewards. However, the rate's dependence on the dimensionality of the context space, compared to traditional linear bandit rates, remains unclear. In our research, we provide a new analysis revealing that the established inequality is applicable even when the context space has a high-dimensional structure. Additionally, we create a lower bound to extend the existing rate bound in a non-trivial manner, demonstrating that the established rate is nearly optimal for certain high-dimensional scenarios. To surpass the upper bound, we develop a linear contextual bandit algorithm of a new type, which yields a near-optimal rate when combined with a specific data processing technique. When applied to a linear bandit model without contexts, this algorithm offers a superior rate of of 4.5ln(T)/\Delta^2. Our results extend beyond linear contextual bandits to the broader class of linear situational bandits. Our main contribution lies in the discovery that, with a specific data processing technique, the existing rate bound can be matched for a wide range of situational bandit settings, which in turn enables the development of efficient algorithms for these settings. Our research also explores a linear situational bandit setting with changing situations to provide an improved upper bound and a nearly tight lower bound, which in turn yields an efficient algorithm with a near-optimal rate. Our findings are further illustrated through simulations, which validate our theoretical results. Our research is the first to consider the challenging problem of learning in distributed linear situational bandits without sharing the context space and provides a solution that yields a near-optimal rate. This article will present an alternative proof of a recent integer equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ having no solutions for $n<12$, and we will also demonstrate that this solution cannot be achieved through the application of standard techniques used to tackle similar Diophantine equations, such as converting them into quadratic forms and employing the methods of Baker-Chowla and W.M.S. van der Poorten, or alternatively, utilizing the large sieve inequality and its variants to examine the solutions for $(a,b)$ for a given $n$. Additionally, we will discuss the potential connection between this particular equation and the existence of solutions to another related Diophantine equation, also of a quadratic nature. Moreover, we will explore the possibility of this equation being linked to another problem related to the growth pattern of Pascal's triangle. Finally, we will examine and validate the solutions to the original Diophantine equation for $n \leq 300$. Notably, we discovered that the solutions to this equation are limited to the set $\{ (0,0), (1,1), (2,2), (4,4), (7,7)\ }$ for $n=12$, and for $n>12$, the smallest possible pair $(a,b)$ exceeds $10^6$ for $n=23$, and $10^{14}$ for $n=300$. Moreover, we established a lower bound for the solutions to this equation of a specific form, which is equivalent to solutions to another related Diophantine equation, ultimately providing insight into the rate of growth of this particular Diophantine equation.

Hierarchical representations are a fundamental aspect in information retrieval and knowledge management, enabling effective categorization and navigation of complex taxonomic structures. Although various methods exist for determining the relationships between nodes in a flat network, few strategies are available to identify the relative positions of elements within a layered system. This research addresses this limitation by introducing an expansion model that utilizes non-linear associations to determine the hierarchical connections among elements in a system. Unlike traditional multilinear methods, this approach can distinguish between linear and circular relationships, thereby preventing infinite feedback loops. Furthermore, by accounting for non-unique representations, the model can determine the relative precision of different hierarchies constructed from the same data set. Experimental evaluations using synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing benchmarks in reconstructing accurate hierarchies and identifying key nodes in networks. The model's versatility in capturing non-linear associations also enables it to be applied effectively in real-world applications such as knowledge graphs and semantic web protocols. The code for the proposed method has been made publicly available on GitHub. Despite its effectiveness, there are areas for further improvement, including enhancing the model's scalability for large networks and developing a representation learning framework similar to multilinear autoencoders. These limitations present opportunities for future research in this domain. A key challenge in quantum annealing lies in creating suitable gaps between the initial Hamiltonian's degeneracy and its minimization, particularly when encountering Ising models with extensive degeneracy in the initial state. Here, we develop a modified quantum annealing framework that leverages combined application of quantum annealing and time-dependent driving forces to create temporary separations between the initial state's degenerate manifolds, facilitating solution identification even in instances where individual quantum annealing processors cannot determine the outcome. As an illustrative example, we employ this method in solving a randomly generated precise cover problem, simulating an experiment that would be feasible with a real D-Wave 2000Q processor. The resulting data demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, illustrating how the quantum annealing interval's optimal choice can significantly enhance solution success rates and precision. As an important practical insight, our findings reveal that in real-world applications, successful quantum annealing can often fail due to insufficient gap creation rather than insufficient quantum annealing time. As a practical consequence, this knowledge enables the efficient re-use of failed quantum annealing data by applying a simple time-dependent driving correction, thereby regaining valuable solution samples from discarded data. The most effective quantum annealing interval proves to be directly related to the problem's underlying degeneracy, offering a universally applicable guideline for the re-analysis of failed quantum annealing data in a wide range of combinatorial optimization problems. The combined application of time-dependent driving and quantum annealing proves particularly beneficial in solving problems that, when formulated using the standard quantum annealing framework, result in insufficient solution success rates and precision. As an illustrative numerical example, we simulate a realistic experiment involving a D-Wave 2000Q processor, demonstrating how the combined application of time-dependent driving and quantum annealing can recover solution precisions and success rates in the precise cover problem. The resulting quench dynamics' periodic four-state cell structure reveals valuable insights into the combined application of time-dependent driving and quantum annealing, specifically highlighting the crucial role of inter-state coupling as it influences the combined framework's solution recovery effectiveness. The observed periodic four-state cell structure also provides a previously unreported answer to the open question of whether and how the precise cover problem's discrete periodic dynamics can be captured using time-dependent driving forces. As a broader consequence, the developed combined application of time-dependent driving and quantum annealing can be suitably generalized for use in recovering solution recovery in a wide range of combinatorial optimization problems featuring complex, periodic quench dynamics induced by time-dependent driving forces.

A phenomenon known as vertical shear instability (VSI) occurs in protoplanetary disk systems and is thought to contribute significantly to the enhancement of solid particles and chemical compounds. However, it's also believed that the growth of dust particles can impact the VSI, potentially suppressing it, which in turn could limit the distribution of particles and chemicals. In our study, we examined the influence of particle growth on VSI by simulating and analyzing the development of 1-micron particles made of silicate in a model solar nebula. We utilized both linear stability analysis and nonlinear simulations to investigate the VSI in a region with temperatures ranging from 1000K to 500K. Our findings reveal that the growth of particles can indeed hinder VSI but is relatively ineffective at higher temperatures. In these ranges, growing particles only slightly slow the VSI's growth rate and have a minimal impact on their saturation levels. On the other hand, at lower temperatures, the particles' growth rate exceeds their migration rate, which could potentially halt the VSI's growth and even lead to its decay. In our research, VSI became non-existent at temperatures below 350K. This research focuses on harmonic functions within a specific context and expands a notable result by Liang and Zheng. It establishes the Liouville theorem for a class of fixed scalar curvature manifolds and provides an alternate proof for a previously established theorem by Guan and Liang. Additionally, it offers an important estimate that facilitates the solution to a nonlinear Monge-Ampere equation used in a priori assumption for local solvability, similar to an earlier approach by Xiang. This, in turn, enables us to prove local uniform bounds for a specific type of Monge-Ampere equations, which are a crucial step in solving global solvability issues. To illustrate the utility and feasibility of these results, we incorporate them into an existing proof for global solvability of a specific Chern-Conformal Kang-Si-Yang equation, which provides an alternative solution to an earlier, more complex approach. Lastly, we discuss some further generalizations and possible related results. This research was presented at the 2021 International Conference on Geometry and Mathematics, held in Kyoto, Japan.

Multi-head attention based models like Transformers have been successfully applied to various tasks including classification, where a classification head is placed on top of the encoder output. However, using separate attention mechanisms for each class has been shown to be less effective than shared attention for many situations. In this work, we explore alternatives to multi-head classification models and present a simple, effective approach using dynamic entrances with global mean pooling, which outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods on several classification benchmarks. When applied to sound event detection, our method achieves comparable results to current methods but with significantly reduced parameters. Furthermore, we find it to be highly successful when used for classification of long sequences and images, achieving state-of-the-art results on CIFAR-100 and obtaining 95.63% accuracy on a custom 10-class speech command classification benchmark consisting of long mel spectrogram sequences. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub.

High-accuracy measurements of parallax by missions like Gaia rely on a solid understanding of general relativity. A key area of uncertainty stems from the limited knowledge of certain post-Newtonian parameters, particularly $\gamma$, which affects the calculation of parallax distances. By considering various scenarios of Gaia-like observations, we've examined how a broader range of post-Newtonian parameters influence the precision of parallax measurements. Our results indicate that a more precise value of $\gamma$ is crucial for maximizing the accuracy of parallax measurements, with a target value of at least $10^{-5}$ for a precision of $10^{-3}$. Furthermore, we've explored the connection between the PPN $\gamma$ parameter and other post-Newtonian variables, identifying a potential relationship that could facilitate a more nuanced understanding of its impact on measurements. By accounting for the Gaia mission's ability to measure the PPN $\gamma$ parameter through ecliptic latitude variations, we anticipate a precision of $0.0005$ in $\gamma$ measurements, which would minimize the impact on parallax distance precision to $0.5\%$. Overall, our analysis underlines the significance of determining the PPN $\gamma$ parameter with higher precision to further enhance the accuracy of parallax distance measurements.

To break down the difficulties in achieving human-level performance on comprehensive, unseen questions, it's vital to analyze the underlying semantics by tracing the paths of relevant knowledge. Presently, the prevailing method involves focusing on individual answer production, without exploring the underlying semantic connections. We introduce a novel approach, called SCCF, that delves into the semantic associations between intermediate knowledge connections, providing a platform to explore, analyze, and even intervene in the knowledge pathways. By examining the intermediate representations, we can pinpoint the contributing knowledge entities and even inject new information to influence the response production. Empirical evaluations on the CCSQ dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of SCCF in capturing the intrinsic semantics of question answering, surpassing the state-of-the-art baselines by a significant margin. Moreover, SCCF showcases the potential for interpreting complex question answering through the lens of semantic analysis, taking one step closer to grasping the intricate relationships between knowledge, semantics, and language. The code is available online at this link: https://github.com/ChengmingXu/SCCF.

A systematic examination of available spectra for cometary molecules has revealed a lack of data for 11 out of 17 oxygen-containing molecular cations. These deficient measurements are most prominent in the 200-400 nm range and could significantly impact the analysis of ancient cosmic rays, influencing our understanding of their sources and the composition of primordial gas. Furthermore, the limited information hinders accurate calculations of electron impact excitation and ion-neutral reactions that are crucial for accurately interpreting observations of cometary atmospheres, particularly in regards to the 0.01 Hill sphere region around comets where solid body tides exert a substantial influence and Mars and some asteroids are affected. A new measurement initiative is proposed to address these knowledge gaps and enhance our comprehension of these crucial, ancient cosmic particles. A proposed measurement strategy is outlined to rapidly gather spectra for these missing molecules using a doubleTOF mass spectrometer during a comet flyby, utilizing the sun as a backlight to measure the scattering of electrons within the plume. This approach offers a cost-effective means of gathering the necessary data to address these knowledge deficiencies. FedLearn from diverse data poses a significant challenge due to its heterogeneity, leading to slow convergence and poor performance. To overcome this challenge, we propose a new random stroll method called FedLearn-Journey, which successfully tackles convergence and performance issues by exploring diverse data effectively. FedLearn-Journey breaks down each round into three distinct phases: selecting a subset of clients, determining individual stroll lengths, and calculating optimal weights. We establish that this approach results in faster convergence and improved performance compared to standard federated learning. Moreover, we demonstrate that FedLearn-Journey yields superior outcomes when compared to alternative stroll methods and traditional federated learning frameworks. We also provide a critical examination of hyperparameters' impact on performance, discovering that a carefully chosen phase structure leads to optimal results. To facilitate seamless deployment on real-world applications, we provide concrete guidelines for selecting hyperparameters. We put FedLearn-Journey through rigorous testing on synthetic data and real-world datasets, achieving notable improvements in both cases. These enhancements are quantified in terms of convergence speed, accuracy, and robustness. To address scalability issues, we develop an optimized version of FedLearn-Journey called FedLearn-Stroll, which prioritizes lighter strolls and streamlined phase structures, resulting in significant reductions in communication overhead and training duration. We successfully deploy FedLearn-Stroll on complex real-world datasets consisting of millions of data points, achieving notable improvements of up to 300% in both convergence speed and accuracy. These breakthroughs pave the way for secure and scalable training across vast, heterogeneous datasets in real-world settings. We publicly release FedLearn-Journey's code on GitHub.

Research examining the connection between mental health and the criminal justice system highlights the prevalence of mental health issues among offenders. Despite this, there is limited analysis of the effect of compulsory therapy within the justice system on offenders' psychological well-being, particularly ego-integrity and social connection. This study investigates the impact of compulsory therapy on the psychological well-being of offenders, with a focus on those nearing the end of their sentences. Utilizing a quasi-experimental design and survey data from 1,200 offenders, researchers discovered that those who received therapy exhibited greater ego-integrity and social connection compared to those who did not. Notably, this effect was more pronounced among offenders who completed their sentences and exited the justice system. The study's findings suggest that compulsory therapy can significantly boost offenders' psychological well-being, with far-reaching implications for the justice system, mental health services, and broader societal benefits. By promoting offenders' psychological well-being, the justice system can reduce recidivism rates and foster more positive community relationships among released offenders. System-level interventions like compulsory therapy can thus yield substantial gains for both individuals and society as a whole. Given the limited resources available within the justice system, prioritizing and investing in such interventions is crucial. Furthermore, the study highlights the value of incorporating measures of psychological well-being into evaluation frameworks for justice system interventions. By doing so, researchers and policymakers can gain a more nuanced understanding of the effects of these interventions and make more informed policy decisions. A persistent challenge in healthcare image segmentation tasks is obtaining a large amount of high-quality training data. To mitigate this issue, researchers frequently leverage semi-supervised techniques to utilize a smaller dataset with more detailed pixel-level annotations. In conjunction with an encoder-decoder architecture, a common approach involves training an encoder to produce a latent representation that matches the distribution of unsupervised, partially annotated data. We propose a novel consistency regularization method that enhances the encoder's ability to produce accurate latent representations when given limited annotations. In essence, the encoder is trained to reproduce the same latent representation for different partially annotated views of the same image. We demonstrate the efficacy of this technique in conjunction with UNET-like architectures in three distinct medical image segmentation applications: liver lesion segmentation from CT and MRI scans and colon polyp segmentation from colonoscopy videos. By conducting thorough experiments on these datasets, we establish that our proposed technique consistently outperforms existing baselines, including an influential UNET-based semi-supervised method, by 2.5% to 6% in terms of Dice coefficient. Furthermore, we find that our proposed technique is highly adaptable and can be effectively integrated with a wide range of UNET-based semi-supervised architectures, yielding comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods that employ complex encoders and decoder architectures. By leveraging our proposed technique in conjunction with a simple UNET architecture, we achieve results on par with the current medical imaging segmentation benchmark. Finally, we provide pre-trained models and segmentation masks for free download on our official website.

The dynamics of complex systems, exhibiting multiscalar chaos, present a significant challenge for time-series based machine learning models. Since these dynamics span various time frames, a single feature extraction method is not effective in capturing their underlying patterns. To address this issue, a novel graph neural network called Temporal Molecular Complex Networks (TMCN) is proposed to capture the molecular dynamics of chemical reactions. This model utilizes molecular graphs to integrate molecular properties and bond information and combines temporal CNNs to capture dynamics on different timescale intervals. By integrating local and global information, TMCN demonstrates superior performance in predicting reaction outcomes in a real-world example. Furthermore, to facilitate real-time applications, the model is optimized for lower computational complexity. The code for this project is available online.
