Knowledge tracing, a technology that predicts students' knowledge based on interactions with educational systems, has gained significant interest recently. The field has seen an explosion of innovative methods and multiple evaluations comparing different techniques have been conducted, however, a unified testing framework for this type of system is absent. This paper presents pyKT, a Python-based testing framework designed to evaluate knowledge tracing systems and other related models. The framework is characterized by three key features: (1) easy integration with existing models, (2) multiple evaluation metrics, and (3) simulated user interactions to test system performance. We demonstrate the benefits of using this framework by conducting a comprehensive evaluation of current deep learning-based knowledge tracing systems using three different architectures. The results show that the StudentKnowledgeTracing model using a memory-based approach outperforms other deep learning-based methods in terms of accuracy and system consistency. The pyKT framework is available for public use, providing a starting point for evaluating and comparing future knowledge tracing systems. The StudentKnowledgeTracing models' code and dataset are also available for public use. When solvers identify an instance that violates a particular constraint, they provide a witness - a formula that, when combined with the original constraint, results in a logically false statement - however, interpreting this witness can be challenging. To enhance the effectiveness of analysis verified by SMT solvers, our research presents Alethe, a universally applicable format for converting witness formulas produced by solvers into evidence that can be easily understood by various stakeholders. We demonstrate the versatility of this format by converting witness formulas into multiple evidence representations that are intelligible to different parties, including humans and machines. To facilitate seamless integration of SMT solvers with various applications, we are making the Alethe format available as an open-source tool on GitHub. To illustrate the versatility of Alethe, we present an empirical evaluation that showcases how converting witness formulas in this format yields beneficial outcomes for multiple tasks, including but not limited to, bug localization, model extraction, and verification conditional debugging. By providing a standardized format for witness formulas and demonstrating its utility in various settings, our research aims to contribute a valuable resource to the verification community that can be used in conjunction with existing solvers to produce more effective and accurate analyses. To this end, we are open to collaborating with developers of SMT solvers and other verified tools to explore additional uses of the Alethe format. By standardizing the format of witness formulas, future versions of solvers can be designed to produce evidence directly in this format, eliminating the need for additional conversion steps and facilitating seamless integration with various applications. To facilitate this goal, we propose a set of guidelines for developers of solvers and other verified tools on how to produce evidence in the Alethe format. As machine learning models grow in size and complexity, the need to reduce communication costs during training has led to the development of efficient federated learning algorithms.  Despite low communication costs, traditional federated algorithms often fail to converge quickly due to limited participant data.  To accelerate convergence, researchers have explored fluctuation-based algorithms that leverage statistical variance to determine learning rates.  However, these methods are often hindered by the requirement for synchronized gradient updates, which can limit participation and lead to biased models in unconstrained datasets.  We address this challenge by introducing a new, synchronized learning framework called Buffered Synchronous Aggregation (BSA), which allows for unconstrained gradients in federated training.  We also develop an optimized version of the algorithm called Optimized BSA (OBSA), which eliminates the need for precise variance estimation.  Through comprehensive testing, we found that both BSA and OBSA achieve comparable performance to non-synchronized algorithms in unconstrained, large datasets.  By leveraging real-world dataset examples and comparing BSA and OBSA to non-synchronized algorithms, we demonstrate that both variants significantly reduce communication costs while maintaining high accuracy. Recent advancements in end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems have made it feasible to develop a unified framework that enables multi-language ASR. In this model, a single neural network is trained to concurrently recognize multiple languages without prior knowledge of the spoken language. Inspired by this work, we explore a related but distinct problem - a single-system ASR that can handle different speech input qualities. Here, we train a neural network to recognize speech with a rough quality and subsequently enhance the recognition output to match the quality of a clean speech dataset. To achieve this, we employ a transfer learning approach that includes two key components: 1) an initial neural network trained on rough-quality speech and 2) a decoder trained on a great deal of clean data. This decoder is trained to take the output from the initial network and produce a more accurate transcription similar to what's obtained from a network trained on clean data. We evaluate this system on the Google Speech Commands v1 dataset and find that it yields a word error rate (WER) of 9.1\%, outperforming a network trained solely on rough-quality speech with a WER of 12.1\%. Similarly, we observe an improvement in WER from 34.1\% to 29.2\% when the input speech transitions from a clean speech to speech with a rough quality. To further expand this system's capabilities, we adapt the network to recognize the Polish language, which requires training the network on little data - only 83 hours of recorded speech. To overcome this limitation, we resort to data augmentation techniques, add considerable amounts of artificially generated speech to the training dataset, and employ a teacher-student training approach to refine the network. In the end, we successfully develop a neural network that can recognize the Polish language with a WER of 22.8\%, a significant improvement over a network trained solely on clean speech data with a WER of 29.6\%. To further analyze the system's performance, we conduct an ablation study and discover that the data augmentation technique accounts for the largest share of improvement in WER (8.5%), followed by the teacher-student training approach (4.5%) and finally the transfer learning from a different language (3.5%). To the best of our knowledge, this work marks the very first attempt to develop a neural network that can recognize the Polish language with such a limited amount of recorded speech. Recent advances in navigation systems for marine robots using acoustic signals have opened up possibilities for deploying robots in complex underwater environments for extended periods. However, underwater robots' ability to navigate is impaired by the slow transmission speed of acoustic signals and the presence of water-borne noise. Additionally, the robots' mobility is limited due to high battery costs and logistical challenges in replacing or recharging them underwater. As a result, there's a pressing need to develop navigation systems that are energy-efficient, silent, and fast. Acoustic communication and sensing technology, also known as acoustic coexistence, enables devices to transmit and receive signals on different frequencies, thus allowing the robot to determine its position using ultrasonic signals. Although this method offers a significant improvement over acoustic-only navigation systems, it introduces new challenges, including the need for a model that can efficiently learn and predict the variation of ultrasonic signals over time. In this work, we developed a novel Gaussian Process model that learns the temporal dynamics of ultrasonic signals with limited training data, achieving a 5-fold improvement in position estimation accuracy compared to a baseline method. Moreover, we demonstrated the energy-efficiency, silence, and speed enhancements of the navigation system in real-world applications, with a 99% reduction in transmission data, a 20 dB reduction in emitted power, and a 3 times increase in data update frequency. As a result, the system can be safely and efficiently deployed on underwater robots for an extended period. As for the future work, we plan to further enhance the model's performance by exploring new directions such as using a different kernel function and incorporating additional features, as well as investigating the applicability of the system to other scenarios, including outdoor environments. By applying an ergodicity assumption and employing a multi-fluid hydrodynamics approach, we derived a dynamic model for the body's rotation and mass distribution. This achievement is particularly significant as it yields a positive and physically interpretable result for the pressure, and it also offers a practical means of approximating the two-fluid body's mass distribution and the velocity of its fluid components. In the context of allocating indivisible goods to self-interested and potentially selfish students, we investigate the possibility of creating a fair and stable allocation system. Specifically, we examine whether there exists an equitable and pure Nash equilibrium allocation structure for any given set of students, goods, and target fairness standards. To tackle this problem, we develop a new notion of equitable allocation, referred to as \emph{agent-wise fairness}, which can be viewed as a variation of the well-known notion of lexicanity. We go on to demonstrate that there is no algorithmic means to determine whether an equitable and pure Nash equilibrium allocation exists for any given instance of student allocation. Moreover, we prove that even a simplified variant of fair allocation, which we call \emph{alternating lexicanity}, fails to guarantee pure Nash equilibria through a carefully constructed example. This serves as a distinguishing feature that differentiates alternating lexicanity from other analogous fair allocation properties, which are known to ensure pure Nash equilibria. We also explore various other variants of fairness and examine their relationship with the existing results. Finally, we discuss the connection between alternating lexicanity and another variant of fairness known as \emph{mean fairness}, and we demonstrate that there is an instance for which the existence of a pure Nash equilibrium alternatingly fair allocation does not imply the existence of a mean fair allocation, whereas the converse does hold. This provides an insight into the distinct characteristics of these two variants of fairness. This research extends upon the prior work conducted by Aardema et al. by offering a new and more intricate fair allocation scenario, which in turn builds upon the initial framework proposed by Bichinger and Ye. It also expands upon the earlier work conducted by an anonymous author. It's worth noting that the results presented in this paper are applicable to any student allocation setting and do not confine to specific contexts such as school or college settings. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is challenging due to the need for diverse data that includes successful interactions. A common limitation of offline datasets is that they often prioritize collecting data from individual agent trajectories over assessing the agent's ability to collaborate effectively with others. As a result, learning from offline data often prioritizes individual performance over social performance. In this paper, a new evaluation metric called cumulative success ratio (CSR) is introduced to assess a single agent's ability to collaborate successfully with others, as indicated by the proportion of positive outcomes in its trajectories. A more challenging problem is then defined as learning from offline data with a focus on maximizing CSR, a problem we refer to as offline multi-agent reinforcement learning from positive trajectories (MARL-PT). To address this challenging problem, a straightforward yet effective approach called positive trajectory augmentation (PTA) is proposed, which involves augmenting the offline dataset with fabricated data that mimics the agent's behavior in new situations. By incorporating the novel PTA module, which selects the most informative data to replicate, a simpler approach is created that can be efficiently trained using just a few parameters. When applied to challenging scenarios, this approach demonstrates superior performance compared to existing methods, as validated by multiple challenging scenarios. When two particles are entangled, a measurement on one particle instantly affects the other, regardless of distance, causing a change in its state. This nonlocal effect can arise even when just one particle is placed within an entangled system, suggesting that the ability to create and manage single-particle entanglement holds significant potential for advancing quantum technology. By leveraging single-particle entanglement, it's theoretically possible to develop precise state measurement and guidance systems for various applications, including quantum communication, quantum computation, and quantum metrology. By combining optical parametric amplifiers with specific types of entangled states known as Bell states, it's been demonstrated both theoretically and experimentally that non-destructive state measurement and guidance can be achieved for a wide range of system sizes, making this technique broadly applicable. Additionally, this method provides a precise means of determining the level of non-destructive state preparation in other systems, giving us a valuable tool for assessing the effectiveness of various state preparation techniques used in a range of quantum technologies.

To extend the possibility of sturdy nonequilibrium steady states in quantum systems beyond one-dimensional cases, we have numerically examined drive-damping scenarios in three-dimensional Hofstadter models using exact diagonalization and matrix product simulations for small and larger lattices, respectively. By controlling the strength of the disorder and drive/damping parameters, we identified regions where sturdy nonequilibrium steady states exist and found that they can occur in both small and larger lattices, differing in their spatial distribution but consistently displaying robust equilibrium-like behavior in specific middle regions of the chain. Furthermore, we found that drive-damping strong enough to overcome the influence of disorder or next-neighbor interactions is required to achieve sturdy nonequilibrium states, demonstrating that in these situations, local information can accurately capture the behavior of the whole system. To validate our findings, we compared the results from both numerical methods used and observed that they yield identical nonequilibrium state properties, thus ensuring the reliability of our conclusions. To better understand the behavior of the Hofstadter model in various situations, we calculated the nonequilibrium cluster decay rate as well as the nonequilibrium correlation length for both bonded and anti-ferromagnetic Heisenberg lattices, and found that in the presence of drive and damping, the system exhibits sturdy nonequilibrium surface and bulk flows, with the flow rate varying with the lattice size but consistently displaying power-law dependencies on the disorder, drive, and damping parameters. Finally, we discuss the possibility that the Hofstadter model can serve as a platform for investigating the possibility of sturdy nonequilibrium states in continuous time, using the bond-anti-ferromagnetic Heisenberg Hamiltonian as a specific example.

One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 moves per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.

To demonstrate its potential, we utilized TextWorldExpress to evaluate the language understanding capabilities of a state-of-the-art language model by testing it through various text-based games, and discovered a notable correlation between better performance in the text-based games and higher real-world language understanding scores. In line with this, we examine the postulate that convex combinations of charged states remain unchanged under the conformal mapping C, ensuring the preservation of irreducibility. We then investigate the implications of this hypothesis for the properties of the conformal net of charged states and observe that it would necessarily result in the equivalence of the conformal net to the algebra of bounded functions, a scenario that contradicts the fundamental assumption that the conformal field theory is local. Consequently, the Feeble Gravity Conjecture would be inaccurately described if it were stated as the conviction that local conformal field theories contain charged states with which one can form convex combinations. Instead, we could rephrase it as the conviction that local conformal field theories contain charged states whose convex combinations remain unchanged under the conformal mapping C, and whose conformal net is equivalent to the algebra of bounded functions, a property that we have demonstrated is inconsistent with the local property of conformal field theories through the application of Doplicher-Haag-Kastler theory. In this study, researchers examined a clinical trial data using Bayes factors to investigate the connection between a specific biomarker and the treatment effect. A statistical model was developed to estimate this relationship and calculate Bayes factors to support or reject the hypothesis of a treatment-biomarker interaction. Multiple trials were combined to increase the power to detect this interaction. The study showed that an approach called "pre-specify, but be prepared to learn" is effective in identifying interactions and reducing Type 2 errors. This approach involves specifying a range of possible Bayes factors thresholds to determine the treatment effect's significance in each trial. If a trial produces a Bayes factor within this range, it is considered significant. If not, the researchers can use the Bayes factor distribution from the non-significant trial to estimate the treatment effect's size. This approach is beneficial because it allows researchers to learn more about the treatment-biomarker interaction during the trial without stopping it or changing the protocol. This strategy can also be applied to other research areas that involve biomarker analysis. This study demonstrated the "pre-specify, but be prepared to learn" approach by examining the Bayes factor distribution from 29 previous trials, which collectively enrolled over 12,000 participants. These trials tested various treatments for different medical conditions and multiple biomarkers. This approach enabled the detection of a treatment-biomarker interaction in approximately 10% of the trials, which met a certain Bayes factor threshold. This study showed that combining multiple trials can detect interactions even with small effects and demonstrated the "pre-specify, but be prepared to learn" approach's effectiveness in identifying these interactions. This approach can be an efficient way to learn about the treatment-biomarker relationships during the trial without stopping it or changing the protocol. This study also discussed the potential drawbacks of this approach, including the difficulty of estimating the Bayes factor distribution from a single trial and the need for large sample sizes to calculate accurate Bayes factor distributions. This study proposed several methods to address these challenges, which can be applied to other research areas that involve biomarker analysis. Our approach, DiscSense, takes a more comprehensive approach by simultaneously investigating discourse indicators and session-wide properties using machine learning models. DiscSense's initial experiment, using a novel set of features and a carefully crafted dataset, demonstrates the predictive value of both local indicators and conversation characteristics and highlights the significance of integrating both contexts for accurate predictions about dialogue outcomes. By successfully integrating two previously distinct research areas, our work paves the way for exploring relationships between local interactions, conversation dynamics, and overall success in talks. By seamlessly integrating both contexts, our findings encourage further investigation into the intricate relationships between the individual elements and the overarching structure of conversations. Moreover, DiscSense's capability to assess discourse indicators across transcripts can be utilized for pedagogical purposes, offering actionable feedback to conversation instructors on areas such as turn management, laughter, and sidetracks. Deep learning models, specifically Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), have achieved high accuracy but are highly susceptible to hardware failures that can cause sudden, permanent damage and trigger attacks. To enhance the security of CNNs, we propose a novel method that focuses on range monitoring of activations across the network. We believe that, given properly trained models, it should be possible to guarantee the presence of specific activation ranges throughout the network, thus preventing overflows that can lead to denial-of-service attacks. To validate this hypothesis, we conducted experiments using a commonly used CNN architecture for image classification and observed that, with some adjustments, we can ensure the presence of desired activation ranges across the network. Furthermore, our proposed method demonstrates improved resilience to hardware failures when compared to an unaltered CNN. We achieved this by utilizing a reduced precision for the network's data types while maintaining the same accuracy as the original CNN. We also tested our method against both intentional and unintentional hardware failures and observed a significant improvement in the network's ability to function correctly. To facilitate real-world implementation, we developed an efficient hardware-friendly activation range monitoring mechanism that requires minimal additional hardware resources. Developing multilingual shared frameworks that integrate multiple languages is a challenging task, primarily because it requires aligning diverse linguistic structures and semantic conventions. We propose a novel approach, Cluster-consistent Word Representation (CWR), to create a shared semantic framework that seamlessly integrates languages by aligning similar concepts and distinguishing different ones. In contrast to conventional methods that solely focus on aligning words and exploiting monolingual data, CWR leverages a unique hybrid strategy that combines word clustering and optimization to ensure the representation captures both intra- and inter-language differences. We utilize a carefully crafted evaluation metric that considers both the similarity and distinctness of word representations to assess the effectiveness of CWR. Our results show that CWR yields substantial gains in distinguishing words in different clusters (F1 score: 72.3%) and maintains a high level of performance in capturing semantic relationships (Pearson correlation: 0.63). When applied to multiclass classification tasks, CWR achieves a notable improvement (average F1 score: 25.6%) compared to baseline methods. Our approach achieves a balance between capturing shared and distinct semantic conventions in a multilingual setting, paving the way for further exploration into the implications of these conventions on linguistic structures and semantic conventions. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/chenxu2016/CWR.

In late October 2019, violent protests and widespread unrest gripped Chile, affecting nearly every aspect of daily life for weeks. A unique feature of this event was the rapid decline in protests and resulting violence as COVID-19 took hold in the country in 2020. Previous studies attributed this decline to increased fear of public gatherings and associated protest-related violence during the pandemic. We sought to explore this hypothesis further by modeling the protests as a non-global epidemiological event. By integrating protest participation and associated violence into a Susceptible-Infected-Recovered (SIR) model and accounting for changes in behavior in response to increased infection risk, we were able to replicate the observed decline in protests and related violence in 2020. Notably, our model highlights the significance of changes in individual behavior in explaining this historical event, in addition to general population-level factors. Additionally, we found that the protests themselves did not significantly impact the spread of COVID-19 in this model, which is consistent with real-world data. Finally, we outline the limitations of our model, including its failure to capture key economic and social drivers of the protests, and suggest potential avenues for model improvement. This research develops an automated method for solving congruence identities involving extended regular expressions (EREs). These expressions extend traditional regular expressions by incorporating the operators of intersection and complement. The presence of the complement operator necessitates a more intricate approach than standard regular expression congruence solving. The proposed solution utilizes a combination of a Brzozowski-style regular expression differentiation and a resolution-based method to dispense with unnecessary variables. By leveraging this approach, we can efficiently determine whether a given ERE equals the universal set. The development of a solver tool, along with a set of presented solving scenarios, demonstrates the effectiveness of this method. The research also explores connections between the proposed solver and decision-making capabilities for first-order logic with regular constraints. The ability to convert first-order logic formulas to equivalent regular expression forms enables straightforward decision-making. The paper further explores the relationship between the solver and the theory of partial order, demonstrating that the solver can distinguish ordered expressions and thereby determine if two expressions are order-equivalent. The development of a solver tool, available online, allows for the conversion of regular expressions to their corresponding ordered forms, thereby providing a straightforward method for defining regular languages based on order constraints. Estimating the state, orientation, and position of a camera-inertial system has numerous practical applications, especially in search and rescue missions. In such scenarios, adding extra sensors or a global positioning system can provide more accurate results but may pose safety risks and increase costs. This paper presents a state estimation method for a monocular camera and inertial measurement unit (IMU) without the need for an initial orientation estimate and with unknown intrinsic camera parameters. Unlike existing methods, we employ an external memory module and recurrent connections to capture dynamic observations, achieving state-of-the-art results in navigation. Moreover, our method sets a new benchmark for indoor navigation using a monocular camera and IMU without pre-estimated orientation, establishing a foundation for future research in this area. The proposed algorithm is tested on public datasets, demonstrating superior performance compared to the current navigation standards. The code for this research is available online.

This approach involves a direct solution to the original partial differential equations and an iterative solution to the inverse problem using a Newton-type method. A series of numerical experiments are conducted to assess the proposed method's effectiveness in recovering both conductivities and source terms given incomplete and noisy data. These experiments demonstrate the proposed method's ability to recover both the included and excluded nodes in a variety of test cases. A key observation from these experiments is that the proposed method is highly sensitive to the accuracy of the initial guess used in the Newton-type iteration and that the inclusion of the time-dependent term significantly improves the recovery of the conductivity and source terms. A comparison with a non-iterative approach reveals that the proposed method yields more accurate and physically plausible results when given the same amount of noisy data. A real-world application to electromagnetic induction sensors used in the detection of landmines is also presented. Most current federated learning methods aim for aggregating models to achieve a balance between accuracy and communication efficiency by conducting optimization-based updates, though these approaches typically prioritize model representation similarity over classification performance. In contrast, this research introduces a new framework called FEDIL, which employs a discriminative model to determine the optimal combination of local models based on their distinctive characteristics, and yields a centralized model that surpasses the individual local models in terms of classification accuracy. By leveraging a combination of local models that exhibit complementary characteristics, FEDIL demonstrates its potential in tackling challenging classification tasks involving concept drift and data imbalance. Moreover, the framework features an adjustable design that permits trade-offs between performance and data privacy protection. Experimental evaluations conducted using real-world datasets reveal that FEDIL achieves a 12.6% improvement in classification accuracy compared to the baseline federated learning method, along with a 30% reduction in communication overhead compared to the baseline optimization-based approach. We examine the rank growth of elliptic curves within the family of quartic extensions over the rationals, focusing on fields extended by a quartic field with Galois group $S_4$ and those with Galois group $A_4$. By utilizing Kummer theory and linking it with the properties of Hilbert symbols, we establish estimates for the minimal rank and the average rank of elliptic curves within these families. This paper outlines the long-term evolution plans for a model of Venus' atmosphere, incorporating the interactions between the atmosphere, mantle, and crust, as well as geological processes that shape the surface. This approach has already yielded notable insights into the gradual development of Venus over time, revealing distinct periods of planetary evolution and pinpointing the timing of key events that have left their mark on the planet. These findings are being presented at the ongoing workshop in Nagoya, Japan.

To enhance the precision of the calculation for the anomalous magnetic moment of the tau neutrino, a detailed examination of the electric dipole form factor of the tau particle is conducted by the authors.  A comprehensive compilation of existing data for $e^+e^-\to \tau^+\tau^-$ was carried out to determine the $|d_{\tau}|$ by utilizing a phase-space factorization approach.  The findings were analyzed under various assumptions to limit the impact of hadronic uncertainty.  The results indicate an upper bound of $1.8\times 10^{-19}$ C·cm for $|d_{\tau}|$ with a relatively small uncertainty of 0.2.  This study also explored the possibility of measuring the $|d_{\tau}|$ in future experiments at the B-factories.  To do so, the authors simulated two possible production processes for $\tau^+\tau^-$ at the energy bands 0.5 to 1.5 GeV above the threshold for $e^+e^-\to \tau^+\tau^-$ to determine if there are accessible channels for calculating the $|d_{\tau}|$ with a given precision for the tau neutrino.  The simulations revealed that scattering channels off the $\tau$ electroweak gauge bosons (such as $\gamma$, $Z$, $W^+$) are more effective for determining $|d_{\tau}|$ compared to the hadronic scattering channels.  The required precision for $|d_{\tau}|$ needed to be achieved by the future neutrino mass measurement experiments at the B-factories was found to range from $10^{-19}$ to $10^{-18}$ C·cm.  The results further showed that measuring the $|d_{\tau}|$ with a precision of $10^{-18}$ C·cm for the tau neutrino may be feasible at the future B-factories with the production energy set at 3.5 GeV above the $e^+e^-\to \tau^+\tau^-$ threshold.  The study also found that measuring the $|d_{\tau}|$ with a precision of $10^{-18}$ C·cm for the tau neutrino may be achievable with a relatively small number of integrated luminosity, on the order of 1 to 10 nb$^{-1}$, but further simulation with a more detailed detector simulation is needed to confirm this result. We conducted a photometric and spectroscopic analysis of the unusual Type II supernova SN 2020jfo, examining its optical and near-infrared light curves over a broad range of time scales. Initially, SN 2020jfo exhibited a slow luminosity decline similar to that seen in typical SNe II at early stages, followed by an unusual 50-day bright plateau phase, roughly one-third as brief as typically observed. By comparing SN 2020jfo to known supernovae types, we found it shares some characteristics with Type II-L supernovae but also exhibits similarities with SNe II with shorter plateau phases. To better understand SN 2020jfo's evolution, we created a comprehensive hydrodynamical explosion model incorporating an initial mass range of 13 to 17 solar masses and a specific mixing length parameterization of convection that mimics the protracted cooling phase observed in its light curves. By performing a forward modeling of SN 2020jfo using an interactive multi-code supernova modeling framework, we obtained a good match between the light curves of the model and SN 2020jfo, along with spectra that generally match those observed. However, the model indicates some discrepancy in its cooling phase phase, suggesting that SN 2020jfo's progenitor star may have had a higher mass than initially estimated. Additionally, we found that SN 2020jfo's remnant compact core likely has a mass of 2.8 solar masses, along with a significant amount of hydrogen in the outer layers that were not efficiently expelled by the supernova explosion. Notably, SN 2020jfo shares some striking similarities with the well-studied Type II supernova SN 1970G, with both exhibiting extended light curves, with SN 2020jfo's light curves stretching far beyond those of SN 1970G. Further research into SN 2020jfo's explosion energy, as well as detailed hydrodynamical explosion models, are necessary to gain a more comprehensive understanding of this supernova. Nonetheless, SN 2020jfo presents an intriguing example of a Type II supernova with a protracted light curve that challenges current theoretical models of these events.

We have developed a new numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method is based on a reformulated set of Euler-Poisson equations that we solve using a quasi-Newton method, in conjunction with the Relativistic Rotating Star Solver (RRSS) that provides the exact solutions for comparison. Our new method yields accurate results when compared to the RRSS solutions, with an average difference of 10^-4 when considering the quadratic sum of the differences in mass and angular momentum. We have successfully applied this scheme to calculate equilibrium configurations for rotating stars in both their static and dynamical cases, with mass ratios up to or exceeding 0.9 and with various specific angular momentum ratios. Our numerical solutions also conform to known analytical properties of rotating stars, and we have further tested our method by simulating a sequence of rotating star configurations and analyzing the resulting relations between their masses, radii, and moment of inertia. The next generation of gravitational wave detectors will yield a vast number of signals from merging neutron star-black hole (NSBH) binaries, but the low signal-to-noise ratio of many detections will limit their effectiveness. To overcome this challenge, machine learning algorithms can be utilized to analyze large datasets for promising candidates. We developed a multi-step deep learning framework to identify and categorize GBM gamma-ray bursts as NSBH binaries based on their gravitational wave signatures. The network consists of three components: a feature extractor to represent gravitational wave signals, a one-class classifier to identify potential binary mergers, and a binary classifier to distinguish between merger binaries and false positives. We trained and tested the network using synthetic gravitational wave signals from BH-BH, NS-BH, and NS-NS collisions, with a separate set of clean signals to calibrate the one-class classifier. The results indicate that the network can accurately distinguish between different types of mergers with a precision of 99% or higher. When applied to a mock LIGO-O3 dataset, the model yields a precision of 99.1% in identifying binary mergers and correctly categorizes 95.6% of NSBH collisions. These outcomes demonstrate the potential of the deep learning framework in efficiently analyzing future gravitational wave datasets for NSBH candidates. Although optimized for a specific set of simulation models, the network's modular structure enables it to be easily adapted to detect other binary merger types. By integrating the model with current pipelines used to analyze gravitational wave data, we can significantly reduce the number of signals that require further analysis, making it possible to detect the same number of signals from future gravitational wave detectors with a reduced computing power. To facilitate this integration, we provide pre-trained models suitable for real-time analysis on GPUs. To evaluate the performance of the models on real LIGO data, we applied them to mock injection data presented in LIGO Scientific Collaboration and Virgo Collaboration, arXiv:2108.10135v2, and found that the precision of identifying binary mergers is 98.3% and the precision of correctly categorizing NSBH collisions is 94.2%. To further improve the efficiency of current pipelines used to analyze gravitational wave data, we open-sourced the deep learning framework used in this study. Mitigating the spread of COVID-19 through social distancing measures significantly reduced urban interactions, resulting in a decline in virus transmission rates but adverse effects on mental and physical health. By analyzing mobile phone data from a large population in Sao Paulo, Brazil, this study reveals that lower-income individuals experienced a more substantial decrease (38% versus 28%) in daily interactions compared to higher-income individuals. This disparity persisted even after controlling for work-related interactions. As a consequence, the existing gap in daily interactions widened by 3.3 percent over the course of the pandemic, exacerbating existing social and economic inequalities. This study highlights the unintended outcome of public health policies aimed at reducing income inequality but inadvertently worsened existing disparities in this instance. By examining past data, the researchers also found a similar pattern of reduced interactions during the 2014 FIFA World Cup, with a similar increase in the existing gap of 3.4 percent over the same period. This study's findings have implications for mitigating the negative health effects of future pandemic-like events by targeting lower-income populations and developing strategies to maintain essential urban interactions while minimizing the risk of transmission. A unified framework for massive star formation proposes that extremely massive stars born directly from cloud cores do not exist and all of them are formed from accumulated material from lower-mass precursors. Although this notion is plausible, it lacks a clear basis in observation. By examining the evolution of massive protostellar cores using a 1.3 mm continuum survey, it is possible to explore the birth pathways of massive stars and investigate core accumulation as a possible pathway. By tracking the movement of massive protostellar cores in the mass and radius plane, researchers found that while some cores follow a single growth pathway at a controlled rate, others exhibit more complex behavior characterized by rapid accumulation phase followed by a contraction phase, which could be influenced by the presence of an interior energy source or another factor. These latter cases have a more significant impact on stellar mass, suggesting that they may give birth to the most massive stars with the shortest lifetimes and potentially influencing the upper limit of stellar mass. In addition, researchers found evidence of the collision of two dense cores that could lead to the formation of extremely massive stars and, as a result, may influence the upper limit of stellar mass and the characteristics of supernovae that follow. These findings, which cover a time span of 0.01 to 500 years, provide new insights into the birth mechanisms of massive stars, the timescales involved in their formation, and the possible locations where they are born. They also highlight the dynamic nature of the process and the possible role of core collisions in forming the most massive stars. If confirmed, these findings could have significant implications for the study of massive star formation, the formation of binary systems, the upper limit of stellar mass, extreme mass ratio binary formation, and the characteristics of supernovae that follow. This research investigates how water waves propagate in the presence of a uniform vertical vorticity forcing a long-crested irregular wave train. We develop a Hamiltonian Hamilton-Dysthe formula that describes how the wave spectrum evolves over time, taking into consideration the effects of uniform vorticity, water depth, shoreline constraints, and a weak dissipation force. We then compare our predicted formula to results obtained through direct numerical simulations of the full water wave problem, finding that the predicted formula accurately predicts the shift in the peak frequency of the wave spectrum and accurately models the occurrence of wave breaking, although it overestimates the rate of change of the wave energy spectrum by a constant factor. We also find that removing the uniform vorticity term in the predicted formula yields a good approximation of the original Hamilton-Dysthe formula, both in its linear and nonlinear forms. We believe that our results have implications for mitigating the effects of uniform vorticity on the evolution of wave spectra, and that they pave the way for further study of more complex scenarios, such as waves in the presence of multiple vortices or rotating water. We conclude by outlining potential research directions for extending our findings in these areas.

Autonomous underwater vehicle navigation faces significant challenges due to limited sensing capabilities, restricted communication options, and harsh underwater environments. Underwater acoustic communication is slow and unreliable, necessitating vehicles to operate independently for extended periods. To enhance the mobility of these vehicles, various schemes have been proposed to optimize path planning and reduce exploration time while discovering an area. In this study, a novel navigation strategy called stratified coverage is presented, which aims to maximize discovery coverage while minimizing the surface area that the vehicle must break through to resurface for fresh air. To achieve this, the algorithm focuses on identifying the optimal navigation depth to maximize exploration efficiency. To further boost discovery efficiency, it recommends an uneven division of the searched area, prioritizing regions closer to the water's surface for exploration. To put this idea into practice, we developed a real-time sonar integration module for navigation control that combines sonar and pressure sensor data to determine the vehicle's position and altitude. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method, we conducted extensive simulations and a real-world experiment using an underwater vehicle equipped with a pressure sensor and a scanning sonar. The results show that our proposed method leads to a 50% reduction in discovery time and a 25% decrease in the area that the vehicle must break through to resurface for fresh air. To facilitate replication, the code for the real-time sonar integration module and the navigation controller has been made publicly available. Verifying news accuracy has become increasingly difficult in the social media age. False news spread quickly and are difficult to track, posing significant issues for individual safety and societal trust in media. This paper proposes an innovative method to aid in identifying false news by condensing articles about the same event into a single, unified document. We utilize a neural network to automatically condense articles, selecting those that mention the same topic. My approach involves training a set of features on a subset of articles and calculating a similarity score for each remaining uncondensed article. Articles with a high similarity score are combined with the features to form a condensed document. We gather and label a dataset of articles that mention the same topic but have different levels of truthfulness. Each article in the dataset is paired with a corresponding condensed document, except in cases where a false article's similarity to the true ones is artificially decreased to mimic real-world conditions. We train and evaluate several machine learning models on this dataset, finding that condensing articles about the same event enhances the accuracy of several models in detecting false news. However, the impact of condensation varies depending on the features used to train the models. We also gather a larger, more complex dataset of articles about different topics, selecting those that mention the same event but are differing levels of truthfulness. We train and evaluate several models on this dataset, discovering that the best-performing model is a complex neural network that outperforms a straightforward baseline by over 10%. In recent years, AI models have significantly improved in answering natural language questions, but they have not been effective in modifying question tags to target users' emotional needs. To address this limitation, we developed a method to automatically adjust question tags to capture the emotional content intended by the askers. In this study, we applied our proposed method to emotional-connected questions and evaluated its performance, discovering that it excels in both tag adjustment and sentiment prediction tasks compared to alternative approaches. To further validate our method's utility, we conducted an averted experiment in which we manipulated participants' emotional states while asking questions and found that the tag adjustment method we developed successfully captured their intended emotional content. To facilitate future research and practical applications, we openly released our code and data on sentiment prediction and tag adjustment for the sake of academic progress.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to describe the localized spin states formed at metal surfaces by 4d and 5d magnetic adatoms and dimers. This model, based solely on initial principles, accurately explains the spectral characteristics of YSR states and provides a clear understanding of how superconducting properties influence the localized spin states. Utilizing a $T$-matrix approach and taking into account the effects of electron-electron interactions and spin polarization of the Yu--Shiba--Rusinant states, a comprehensive analysis has been performed of Mn monomers and dimers on a Nb(110) surface within a $k$-space formulation. This has allowed for a detailed examination of how the spin polarization of YSR states changes with the distance between dimerized magnetic moments, as well as the influence of the superconducting properties of the host material, in a manner that is relevant to scanning tunneling microscopy measurements. This theoretical framework has been applied to previously unexplained data related to the magnetic polarization of YSR states in Mn monomers and and dimers on a Nb(110) surface, with excellent agreement between calculated and experimental results. To fortify the discovery of the top quark's elastic production at the Large Hadron Collider, we propose analyzing the rapidity difference between the two protons detected beyond the main scattering body. This analysis targets the high-mass region of 1.4 TeV, where the elastic top quark pair production cross-section is most prominent, and we suggest a data selection for the forward proton detectors that prioritizes events with large proton rapidity gaps and limited central hadronic activity. By focusing on forward-going protons with significant transverse momentum and high-mass elastic scattering, we aim to extract the signal of top quark pair production in an entirely new variable space that is distinct from conventional jet-based searches and can effectively complement them with little overlap. Leveraging this approach on a 5.4 inverse femtobarn dataset at a 13 TeV collision energy, and with the inclusion of simulated detector effects using the DELPHI fast Monte Carlo, we estimate an elastic top quark pair production cross-section of 0.17 nanobarns with an uncertainty of 33 nanobarns, or a top quark pair production probability of 3.4 times 10 to the 4th power divided by barn, with an uncertainty of 6.6 times 10 to the 4th power divided by barn. These findings support the feasibility of detecting top quark pair production at the Large Hadron Collider via elastic scattering in the forward proton region with low overlap to other production channels and in a variable space that differs from conventional jet-based searches.

A stochastic process's persistence can be defined as the duration it spends above a certain threshold. This research examines the one-dimensional random walk model, expanding on previous studies by Guillot to analyze the probability of persistence for an infinite period. A key finding is that there is a critical value, if the process's initial probability is higher than this value, then it will persist forever. This is in contrast to models based on expected duration, which show a unique equilibrium rather than global persistence. Another discovery is that multiple infinite persistence regimes exist, not just the one identified in previous research. This paper also discusses how changing variables affects the model's results and explores similar applications to other stochastic processes. Some of these similar processes exhibit multiple infinite persistence regimes, while others do not. This paper's approach to studying persistence as a function of time includes a numerical calculation using Monte Carlo methods. This allows it to accurately capture complex patterns and provide specific examples, such as a hyperbolic sine function. This research was initially presented at the 2020 INFORMS Annual Meeting. Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, albeit without a clear understanding of their fundamental basis. We investigate the underlying principles of GCNNs by examining their connection to Signal Processing theories, establishing a parallel between spectral convolution in GCNNs and matched filtering in Signal Processing. We leverage this analogy to provide a derivation of the equivalent spatial domain operation, offering a novel perspective on GCNN operations that can be employed across various graph types. Furthermore, we introduce a new GCNN framework that combines spatial and spectral domain operations, resulting in improved performance in comparison to existing GCNN architectures. Experimental results demonstrate the improved efficacy of our proposed method in comparison to standard GCNNs. We also examine the proposed network's scalability and potential for real-world applications by adapting it to analyze complex image scenes. The proposed network's simplicity and efficiency, coupled with enhanced performance, make it an attractive solution for various real-world problems. The code for the proposed method is available online.

In this work, we utilize a $SO(2)$ Chern-Simons gravity theory to demonstrate the existence of spinning hairy black holes and solitons, both of which are equipped with gauge fields, in a scenario where the Higgs phase meets the conformal phase at the horizon of these solutions. By applying the boundary value method in a complex plane, we are able to derive the exact expressions for the Euclidean action, action density, and entropy density of these solutions. Notably, our findings reveal that the Euclidean action exhibits a nontrivial dependence on the complex gauge field, thereby providing a theoretical framework that is in agreement with the physical prediction made by Jensen, Khoury, and Oliwa in 2000. Additionally, our results demonstrate that the Euclidean action can be divided into two distinct components: one that is analogous to the Witten's action and another component that is unique to this scenario. The unique component exhibits a nontrivial dependence on the complex gauge field and offers an alternative explanation for the physical prediction made by Jensen, Khoury, and Oliwa in 2000. Furthermore, our research involves evaluating the Euclidean action for solitons with gauge fields in both the Higgs phase and the conformal phase, both of which yield distinct physical outcomes. The case of the Higgs phase is found to result in a zero Euclidean action, whereas the conformal phase yields a positive Euclidean action that is directly proportional to the complex gauge field. The proportionality coefficient is found to be $2\pi$ after performing a $2\pi$-periodic transformation in the complex gauge field. The positive Euclidean action of the conformal phase provides an alternative theoretical explanation for the positive sign of the soliton's charge, which was initially predicted by Buckley, Jensen, Khoury, and Oliwa in 2000. The unique relationship between the Euclidean action and the complex gauge field that is exhibited by the solitons also offers an alternative explanation for the prediction made by Jensen, Khoury, and Oliwa in 2000, which stated that the solitons' charge must be non-zero. While different representations serve various purposes, they often share a common goal of illustrating algorithms and facilitating understanding between individuals. Despite this common objective, there is no established framework to compare and analyze these representations in relation to each other. In contrast to this diverse set of representations, the field of formal programming languages exhibits a unified approach to algorithmic expression, albeit one that is distant from real-world educational demonstrations. To bridge this gap, we propose developing a high-level language we call "rational pseudocode," one that can be used to generate algorithmic demonstrations and, conversely, can be derived from existing educational content to provide a precise, standardized definition of the presented algorithm. To demonstrate the utility of this approach, we applied the method to a widely used educational example, the bubble sort algorithm, and showed that its underlying structure can be both encoded and decoded with a high degree of accuracy. To expand on this proof, we developed a metric to gauge the similarity between the original and reconstructed pseudocode and used it to investigate multiple algorithmic representations across various fields. This paper introduces a novel strategy for two-player stochastic zero-sum games with imperfect information, where one player pursues and the other withdraws. We divide the state space into hierarchical divisions to solve the game, starting from a high-level representation and gradually refining it to a Markov decision process. Unlike existing methods that focus on a flat state space division, our approach allows for a more efficient representation, capturing complex relationships between states. We demonstrate that any hierarchical division is sufficient to play an $\epsilon$-approximately best response, provided that the number of divisions exceeds a certain threshold that depends on the precision $\epsilon$ and available memory. We also show that algorithms such as hierarchical policy iteration and value iteration can create an optimal policy using a hierarchical division that approximates the ideal division structure. Finally, we show that a specific form of hierarchical division, constructed through clustering based on the similarity of state-action values, results in a policy that is within $\epsilon$ of optimal when the number of clusters exceeds a threshold that depends on $\epsilon$ and other problem features. We validate our results with numerical experiments using randomly generated models and more complex models based on real data. We also explore different models and baselines to evaluate our methods systematically. In recent years, model-driven reinforcement learning for multiple tasks has shown significant promise by consistently delivering high-level performance on a wide range of tasks, even when specific skills have been forgotten due to conflicting goals. We examine this approach in a scenario where tasks are constantly being introduced and others regularly become obsolete, finding that, although initial progress is rapid, the system eventually encounters significant difficulties. We discovered that the disappearance of ancient tasks has an unexpectedly substantial impact and that a vast majority of the system's knowledge becomes endangered within a remarkably short period of time - just 100 new tasks being introduced. To rescue the system, we developed an innovative method of dividing the task space into separate modules, assigning distinct sets of tasks to individual modules. Each module functions independently, allowing the system to explore and learn from a reduced subset of tasks, which significantly reduces learning time and prevents the loss of ancient knowledge. By splitting the tasks into 5 modules or more, we were able to prevent the loss of ancient knowledge and saw a notable improvement in performance on ancient tasks. Moreover, dividing the system in this way also results in improved generalization, enabling the system to perform well even when faced with tasks that are substantially different from those it has been trained on. Recently, graph neural networks have achieved significant performance in various tasks such as node classification and link prediction. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel GNN architecture that utilizes Lorentzian distances to characterize the relationships between nodes. This research examines how a specific variation, known as rational transformations, affects the fundamental invariants derived from relative quantum homology for a particular and well-studied group of functions, known as curve operators. By applying a sophisticated mathematical tool called compactly supported cohomology, we establish a crucial connection that links transformed versions of relative quantum homology to their original forms. This connection is expressed through a specific equivalence based on properties of invariants, invariants derived from the Lagrangian correspondence with itself, and the behavior of monodromy transformations. Ultimately, we demonstrate how this relationship can be utilized to determine various properties of relative quantum homology, including its structure, behavior under change, and relationship with geometric properties. Notably, this leads to an assessment of the contribution of certain specific parameters, known as Maslov degrees, in relation to the geometric properties of curves. This assessment takes the form of inequalities that bound the number of turning points and peaks on curves from below and above, respectively. These inequalities are further refined to include lower and upper bounds for the number of nodes, as well as specific lower and upper bounds for the number of closed components and the number of boundary components, respectively. These results were previously known only in non-rational versions. Additionally, we introduce a new parameter known as genus, demonstrate its relationship to the number of nodes, and derive an upper bound for the Euler characteristic of curves. This upper bound is expressed as a sum of the number of closed components, the number of boundary components, and twice the genus, all of which are known in non-rational versions but were unknown in rational versions. This research also explores the relationship between geometric properties of curves and the parameter $\epsilon_0$ in the Lagrangian correspondence with itself, and shows that $\epsilon_0$ is bound above by twice the Euler characteristic of curves. The safety of radiologists and AI systems can be ensured during radiology tasks by implementing countermeasures to address COVID-19. Although using face masks is common practice, their presence can obscure vital information on patient images, necessitating the development of algorithms to rectify this issue. Here, we propose an innovative method to automatically remove radiologists' face masks from chest X-rays by framing it as an image inpainting task. We employ a combination of U^2-Net and a spatially-adaptive inpainting technique to remove masks from new, unseen data with outstanding results. When evaluating our method on a publicly-available chest X-ray dataset with masks, we find it outperforms existing reference methods according to the PSNR metric by a significant margin of 5.13, demonstrating its superior performance in removing masks from images. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of mask removal on an established chest X-ray disease classification model and discover it has a minimal effect, with an overall accuracy of 94.49% when classifying 13 different diseases with and without removing the masks. With its cutting-edge performance, our method has the potential to be a valuable tool in addressing various illnesses, not just COVID-19. By extending our approach to remove other distracting objects from images, we successfully decrease the false positive rates of the classification model by 7.13% when there are lung lesions present. With its versatility and superior performance, we envision our method being a valuable asset in various clinical settings and emergency situations.
